_meta.description: Plainly's legal & contracts pack. Plain-English meanings for everyday legal documents — leases, contracts, terms of service. Not legal advice; for big decisions, talk to a lawyer.

indemnify.simple: agree to cover someone else's losses
indemnify.detailed: If you indemnify someone, you promise to pay for certain costs, damages, or legal claims they face — often ones caused by your actions. It shifts financial risk onto you.
indemnify.why: An indemnity clause can make you responsible for large, open-ended costs, sometimes more than the deal is worth.
indemnify.next: Find out exactly what you'd be covering and whether there's a dollar cap. Consider asking a lawyer before signing an uncapped indemnity.

limitation of liability.simple: a cap on how much they'll ever owe you
limitation of liability.detailed: A clause that limits how much one side has to pay if something goes wrong — often capped at the amount you paid them, no matter how big your actual loss.
limitation of liability.why: If their service causes you a large loss, this clause can leave you recovering only a small fraction of it.

liability.simple: legal responsibility for harm or loss
liability.detailed: Being legally on the hook for something — usually money owed when someone is harmed or a promise is broken.

arbitration.simple: settle disputes privately instead of in court
arbitration.detailed: A clause that says disagreements are decided by a private arbitrator rather than a public court. The decision is usually final and hard to appeal.
arbitration.why: It often means giving up your right to sue in court or join a class action — and arbitration can favor the company that wrote the contract.
arbitration.next: Check whether arbitration is required and whether you can opt out (some contracts give a short window to do so).

class action waiver.simple: you give up the right to join a group lawsuit
class action waiver.detailed: A promise that you'll only bring claims on your own — never as part of a group of people suing together over the same problem.
class action waiver.why: Group lawsuits are often the only practical way to challenge a big company over small individual harms. Waiving this removes that option.

severability.simple: if one part is invalid, the rest still stands
severability.detailed: A clause saying that if a court throws out one part of the contract, the remaining parts stay in force.

force majeure.detailed: A clause that excuses one or both sides from their obligations when something extraordinary and outside their control happens — like a natural disaster, war, or pandemic.
force majeure.why: It decides who bears the loss when events make the contract impossible to perform. A narrow clause may not protect you in a crisis.
force majeure.next: Check what events are actually listed and whether your situation would qualify.

nda.simple: a promise to keep information secret
nda.detailed: A Non-Disclosure Agreement: a contract where you agree not to share certain confidential information you're given. Breaking it can mean being sued.
nda.why: An overly broad NDA can restrict what you're allowed to say or do for years — read what counts as 'confidential' and for how long.

confidentiality.simple: the duty to keep certain information private
confidentiality.detailed: An obligation to protect specific information and not share it with others outside the agreement.

jurisdiction.simple: which place's courts and laws apply
jurisdiction.detailed: The location whose courts have authority over disputes about the contract. It can decide where you'd have to go to sue or be sued.
jurisdiction.why: If a dispute means traveling to a far-away court, that alone can make it impractical to defend yourself.

governing law.simple: which state or country's laws control the contract
governing law.detailed: The set of laws used to interpret the agreement — for example, 'governed by the laws of Delaware.'

warranty.simple: a promise that something is as described
warranty.detailed: A guarantee about a product, service, or fact — for example, that software will work as described or that goods are free of defects.

disclaimer of warranties.simple: they promise nothing about quality ('as is')
disclaimer of warranties.detailed: A clause saying the product or service is provided 'as is,' with no guarantees that it will work, be accurate, or fit your needs.
disclaimer of warranties.why: If it breaks or fails, you usually can't claim they promised otherwise.

termination clause.simple: the rules for ending the agreement
termination clause.detailed: The part of the contract that says how, when, and by whom the agreement can be ended — and what happens afterward.
termination clause.next: Note how much notice you must give and whether ending early costs you anything.

auto-renewal.simple: the contract renews itself unless you cancel in time
auto-renewal.detailed: The agreement automatically continues for another term unless you give notice to cancel before a deadline. Miss the window and you're locked in for another full period.
auto-renewal.why: People often get charged for a renewal they forgot about because the cancellation deadline passed.
auto-renewal.next: Note the cancellation deadline and notice method now, and set a reminder well before it.

breach.simple: breaking a promise in the contract
breach.detailed: Failing to do something the contract requires (or doing something it forbids). A 'material breach' is a serious one that can let the other side end the deal or sue.

damages.simple: money owed to make up for harm
damages.detailed: The compensation one side pays the other for losses caused by breaking the contract.

liquidated damages.simple: a pre-agreed penalty amount for breaking the deal
liquidated damages.detailed: A fixed sum the contract says you'll pay if you break a specific promise, set in advance instead of calculated later.
liquidated damages.why: You could owe this amount even if the other side's real loss was small — check the number before signing.

waiver.simple: giving up a right on purpose
waiver.detailed: Voluntarily letting go of a legal right or claim — for example, waiving your right to a refund or to sue.

non-compete.simple: a promise not to work for rivals for a while
non-compete.detailed: A clause restricting you from working for competitors or starting a competing business for a set time and area after the deal ends.
non-compete.why: It can limit your future job options — check how long it lasts and how wide the restriction is.

non-solicitation.simple: a promise not to poach their clients or staff
non-solicitation.detailed: A clause stopping you from recruiting the other side's employees or customers for a period after the agreement ends.

assignment.simple: handing the contract over to someone else
assignment.detailed: Transferring your rights or duties under the contract to another party. Many contracts limit when this is allowed.

representations and warranties.simple: facts each side swears are true
representations and warranties.detailed: Statements of fact (representations) and promises (warranties) that each side guarantees — if they turn out false, the other side may have a claim.

covenant.simple: a formal promise to do or not do something
covenant.detailed: A binding commitment within the contract — for example, a covenant to keep insurance, or a covenant not to compete.

consideration.simple: what each side gives to make the deal real
consideration.detailed: The thing of value each party exchanges — money, services, a promise. A contract generally isn't binding without it.

perpetual license.detailed: A right to use something that doesn't expire. Paired with 'irrevocable,' it also can't be taken back.
perpetual license.why: Granting a perpetual, irrevocable license to your content means you can't later change your mind.

intellectual property.simple: ownership of creations like writing, code, or art
intellectual property.detailed: Legal rights over things people create — text, designs, software, inventions, brand names. Contracts often say who owns the IP that's made.

joint and several liability.simple: any one person can be made to pay the whole amount
joint and several liability.detailed: When several people share a debt, this lets the other side collect the entire amount from just one of them — who then has to chase the others for their shares.
joint and several liability.why: You could be forced to cover everyone's portion, not just your own.

statute of limitations.simple: the deadline to bring a legal claim
statute of limitations.detailed: The time limit for suing over a problem. After it passes, you usually lose the right to bring the claim at all.

notice period.simple: how much warning you must give before acting
notice period.detailed: The amount of advance notice required before doing something like cancelling or ending the agreement — e.g. '30 days' written notice.'
notice period.next: Note the exact length and how notice must be delivered (email, letter, portal).

cure period.simple: time given to fix a problem before penalties
cure period.detailed: A grace window to correct a breach after being notified, before the other side can end the contract or take action.

net 30.detailed: An invoicing term meaning the full amount must be paid within 30 days of the invoice date. 'Net 60' and 'Net 15' work the same way with different deadlines.

late fee.simple: an extra charge for paying after the deadline
late fee.detailed: A penalty added when payment is late — sometimes a flat amount, sometimes a percentage that grows over time.

entire agreement.detailed: A clause (also called an 'integration clause') saying the written contract is the complete deal — earlier emails, promises, or verbal agreements don't count.
entire agreement.why: If a salesperson promised something that isn't in the document, this clause can make that promise unenforceable.

data processing agreement.simple: rules for how your data gets handled
data processing agreement.detailed: A contract (DPA) setting out how a company may collect, use, store, and protect personal data on your behalf — often required by privacy laws like GDPR.

acceptable use.simple: the rules for how you're allowed to use a service
acceptable use.detailed: A policy listing what you may and may not do with a product or service. Breaking it can get your account suspended.

personal guarantee.simple: you promise to pay with your own money if the business can't
personal guarantee.detailed: A pledge that makes you personally responsible for a debt or obligation — so if a company can't pay, the other side can come after your personal assets.
personal guarantee.why: This pierces the protection of a business entity and can put your home or savings at risk.
